definition: The overlapping, flattened cells that form the outer layer of wool and hair fibers, with their free edges pointing toward the fiber tip.
explanation: Around the cortex of an animal fiber lies a sheath of cuticle cells that overlap like roof tiles, each exposed edge pointing toward the tip. Each cell is itself layered, with a thin epicuticle outside, then an exocuticle and an inner endocuticle. The outermost surface carries a covalently bound fatty acid layer that makes it water repellent and lowers friction. Because the scale edges all point one way, a fiber slides more easily in one direction than the other. Under moisture, heat and agitation this directional friction lets fibers ratchet past one another and entangle, which underlies felting, fulling and wash shrinkage.
example: Under a microscope, two animal fibers of similar diameter show different scale patterns: one has frequent, prominent scale edges, the other smoother, flatter scales. Students predict which will feel smoother and felt less readily, then compare their observations with fiber identification guides that use scale patterns to help distinguish species. The exercise shows that surface structure, not diameter alone, shapes hand and felting behavior.
caution: Scales are not a defect, and scale patterns vary with species, breed and position along the fiber. Shrink-resist treatments that modify or coat the scales reduce felting but change the surface, so a machine-washable label reflects a treatment rather than the native fiber. Scale pattern is a useful clue for fiber identification but may not settle species on its own without other evidence such as diameter distribution or medullation.
deeper: Wool cuticle cells are roughly 0.5 micrometers thick and point toward the fiber tip. The outermost F-layer of the epicuticle is dominated by 18-methyleicosanoic acid (18-MEA), a methyl-branched fatty acid with 21 carbon atoms that is covalently bound to the protein surface. This is unusual, because most protein-bound fatty acids are straight-chain with an even number of carbons. The 18-MEA layer lubricates the surface, lowers friction and makes the fiber hydrophobic. Directional friction, lower when a fiber moves root-first than tip-first, drives felting. Researchers have also developed quantitative descriptors of scale morphology and found that they correlate with the diffusion coefficient of acid dyes, since the cuticle is the first barrier dye molecules must cross.
origins: Cuticle comes from the Latin cuticula, little skin, a diminutive of cutis. The scaly surface of wool has long been invoked to explain why wool felts while plant fibers do not, and scale patterns remain central to microscopic fiber identification. Studies of the wool follicle have traced how scale patterns form as cuticle cells differentiate, and biochemical work later identified 18-MEA as the major covalently bound fatty acid of mammalian hair fibers, linking surface chemistry to lubricity and water repellency.

definition: Decortication mechanically strips fiber from the surrounding plant tissue: the woody core of bast stems such as hemp and kenaf, or the fleshy pulp of leaves such as sisal.
explanation: The word means removing the outer layer, and in fiber processing it has two related uses. For bast crops, a decorticator breaks the stalk and separates the fibrous outer bast from the woody inner core, called hurd or shiv, often from dry stems that are not fully retted. For leaf fibers such as sisal, which are not normally retted, rotating drums with blades scrape away the soft leaf tissue to free the fiber strands, which are then washed and dried. Ramie is decorticated into ribbons that still need chemical degumming.
example: A hemp farm sends dried stalks to a decortication plant, which returns two streams: bales of bast fiber and woody hurd sold for animal bedding or building materials. A textile buyer asks whether the stalks were retted first, because unretted, decorticated fiber is coarser and more gum-bound and would need further processing before it could be spun into fine yarn.
caution: Decortication is not retting: it separates tissues mechanically rather than breaking down pectin biologically. Fiber decorticated without retting is often suited to industrial uses unless it is further degummed or cottonized. The word is also used in medicine and grain milling with unrelated meanings, and it tells you nothing about fiber fineness or quality.
deeper: In bast stems, fiber bundles lie in the outer tissue, outside the woody core, and are attached to it by pectin-rich tissue. Mechanical decortication applies crushing, bending and impact through fluted rollers, hammers or beaters, so the brittle core fractures while the flexible fiber survives. High-speed hemp decorticators separate hurd from fiber in continuous lines. For sisal and similar leaf fibers, decortication is the main extraction step. Decorticated ramie retains substantial gums and is chemically degummed, typically with hot alkali, before spinning. Outcomes depend on stem moisture, degree of retting and machine settings, with fiber damage traded off against cleanliness.
origins: Built on the Latin cortex, meaning bark, decortication has long meant removing bark, husk or rind. Machine decorticators for fiber plants were developed in the nineteenth century, including early hemp machines in Italy, and mechanical decortication became the standard way to extract sisal. Interest in hemp decortication revived as several countries again permitted industrial hemp cultivation, creating demand for continuous, high-throughput lines.
